{{image-1}}

What I want to talk about is that feeling we can, at times, get after we have done something we deeply regret and what those feelings can lead to depending on our response. By repentance (in the title), I do not intend any special connotations that may be floating in your mind from religious experience, movies, or wherever. I simply mean the act of making a marked change. But I’ll expand on this later. Let’s get into it.

---

There is a deep guttural discomfort that can result from making a horrible choice you regret. Every choice we regret is followed by some discomfort. You pick the wrong ice cream flavor at the store and after seeing what your friend got, you get a little sad. I’m not talking about that. What I mean something more like choices that are followed by sorrow. You mourn having made your choice. You’ve said words you cannot take back, you’ve ruined a lifelong relationship, you’ve lied for too long and it’s caught up to you. It is the feeling you get after you miss hearing the last words of wisdom from a dying loved one because you did not call them when they asked. You were not there when they needed you.

Perhaps you’ve never felt this sorrow before. I will tell you what it is like. It is like wishing you could depart from your own unpleasant company. It is like someone digging a shovel into your stomach and never reaching the bottom. It is holistic embodied regret. And let me say something about how we sometimes think in this mood. We think our choice has changed us forever and mourn the death of who we were before we made it. But I don’t believe this is true. We are the same people we were the morning after we made our choice as we were the morning we made it (consequences aside). The choices we make reflect where we are as people within a certain set of circumstances. Yes there may have been other factors: you were angry, you’ve had a bad month, you were drunk, etc. But no one wakes up and suddenly decides to cheat on their partner. The reality is that life is made up of billions of microchoices that are constantly shaping us. We are like mountains, being shaped by the winds and torrential rains of life. We just keep making choices, only to look up years later to find that they’ve turned us into a kind of person. Now, and this will sound contradictory, this is not to say you are the choice you made, we all make mistakes and there really are exterior factors that helped us make them, but it is also true that your choice did not come from nowhere. And this is why we are so uncomfortable after we’ve made it. You realize that you are not the person that you thought you were and it makes you sorry.

I think there are two main ways you can deal with this discomfort. For one, you can dismiss it. This is the most tempting of the two choices. It’s very easy to dissociate from the choice we regret after we make it. We tell our selves that our choice says nothing about us, it was a fluke, and in reality, had so-and-so been given the same choice, they likely would have made the wrong one as well. This preserves our pristine image of ourselves in our mind and helps us sleep at night. If we just pretend nothing happened, we can move past it, and it’ll all be fine. And while these thoughts help us cope and live with ourselves, they do not make us better people. In fact, over time, it becomes easier and easier to separate our image of ourselves and reality and we become blinded to the latter. So what’s that other choice?

---

Our other option is face what we’ve done with our full selves. We can recognize that our choices do say something about the kind of people we are and are becoming. That no matter how much we envision ourselves as caring and “good” people (whatever that means), our choices sometimes show something different. They reflect a reality inside us that we’d rather ignore, but should not. Because if we own up to how we are, we can change who we’re becoming. It may be time to schedule that therapy session, to stop thinking of ourselves as the hero, or to (God forbid) stop being so self-centered and instead center our lives around life giving connections that actually help us to change (I’m personally a fan of that Jesus guy, he’s a real cool dude). We don’t do these things because lowkenuinely, they are mad uncomfortable. Sitting with the truth of your own brokenness and deficiencies is hard. Making a change takes effort. You will not become a better person by just wishing it so or hitting a yoga session every two weeks. The forces changing you for the better have to be more intentional and at least as potent as the ones that erode your character for the worse. And you owe it to humanity to be that better person. Because someone is sitting on the other side of your choice (sometimes it’s even ourselves), and depending on the one you make, you will leave them better or worse off.

So what’s it going to be?
